entries.name: pair_coll_nonpair_default_oob-errored#0
entries.script: [A1] `Coll((1, 2)).getOrElse(5, true)` — a collection of PAIRS is a `PairOfCols`, whose `getOrElse(i, (L,R))` overrides the interface method with another erasure, so the call goes through a BRIDGE that casts the default to Tuple2. The index is OUT OF RANGE and it still throws: `ClassCastException: class java.lang.Boolean cannot be cast to class scala.Tuple2`, wrapped in an `InvocationTargetException`. **SEPARATING:** an implementation that returns the default here over-accepts.

entries.name: pair_coll_nonpair_default_in_range-errored#1
entries.script: [A2] The same at index 0, IN range. Still throws, and with the same cast — which is the point of the pair: the bridge casts the default before the index is ever consulted. **SEPARATING.**

entries.name: byte_constant_bool_default_oob-errored#2
entries.script: [B1] `Coll[Byte](1,2)` as a CONSTANT, `.getOrElse(5, true)`. `CollOverArray` is `@specialized` and a Coll[Byte] constant carries a static primitive type, so the interface call unboxes the Boolean default: `ClassCastException: class java.lang.Boolean cannot be cast to class java.lang.Byte`. **SEPARATING, and half of the provenance pair** — compare B3, which is the same declared type built differently and RETURNS.

entries.name: byte_constant_bool_default_in_range-errored#3
entries.script: [B2] The same at index 0. Still throws — the unboxing precedes the index, exactly as in A. **SEPARATING, and half of the provenance pair** (compare B4).

entries.name: byte_concrete_bool_default_oob-accept#4
entries.script: [B3] `Coll(1.toByte, 2.toByte)` as a ConcreteCollection, `.getOrElse(5, true)` — **the same declared type `Coll[Byte]` as B1**, built generically rather than from a constant, and it RETURNS `true` at cost 74. **THE OTHER HALF OF THE FINDING:** the JVM's answer depends on where the collection came from. Both sides agree on this row, which is what makes B1's red about provenance rather than about `getOrElse`.

entries.name: byte_concrete_bool_default_in_range-accept#5
entries.script: [B4] The same at index 0: returns `Byte 1` at cost 74, where B2 throws. The pair B2/B4 is the cleanest statement of the finding — identical declared type, identical call, identical index, opposite outcome.

entries.name: tuple3_size-accept#6
entries.script: [C1] `(1, 2, 3).size` as a PropertyCall. A 3-item tuple's value IS a `Coll[Any]`, so this simply works: **3 at cost 23**. **SEPARATING the other way:** an implementation that refuses a tuple receiver here OVER-REJECTS.

entries.name: tuple3_apply-accept#7
entries.script: [C2] `(1, 2, 3).apply(0)` — **1 at cost 44**. Same over-reject risk as C1.

entries.name: tuple3_get_or_else-accept#8
entries.script: [C3] `(1, 2, 3).getOrElse(5, 9)` — **9 at cost 49**, the default, since 5 is out of range on a 3-item tuple. Note it does NOT hit A's bridge problem: a tuple is a plain `Coll[Any]`, not a `PairOfCols`. Same over-reject risk.

entries.name: pair_coll_pair_default_oob-accept#9
entries.script: [A3] `Coll((1, 2)).getOrElse(5, (7, 8))` — **THE CONTROL FOR A**, with a PAIR default. Returns `(7, 8)` at cost 109. It is what shows A1/A2 fail because of the DEFAULT's type and not because the receiver is a collection of pairs.

entries.name: pair_coll_pair_default_in_range-accept#10
entries.script: [A4] The same at index 0: returns the element `(1, 2)` at cost 109. Pairs with A3 to show the index is honoured once the default's type is right.
